item.title: The Swing
item.lesson: A young courtier commissioned this picture with unusually specific instructions: paint my mistress on a swing, pushed by a bishop, with me positioned to look up her skirts. Fragonard wisely demoted the bishop to an unwitting elderly servant, hid the lover in the rosebushes at lower left, and produced the definitive image of the Rococo — the frothy, pastel, pleasure-drunk style of the French aristocracy's last golden afternoon. She kicks off her slipper mid-flight (an old symbol of abandoned virtue); a statue of Cupid holds a finger to his lips. Everything is silk, foam, and complicity. The painting is so charming it takes a moment to notice what it documents: a class so insulated it commissioned oil paintings of its own flirtations, twenty-two years before the Revolution arrived with other plans. The art of the guillotine's future clients, painted at the peak of their unknowing.
item.lookFor: Follow the light: the garden is a shadowy green grotto except for one theatrical sunbeam aimed precisely at the swinging girl — stage lighting a century before electricity.
